OVERVIEW

Designing for a Drone,
Not a Person

Most of Watch Dogs: Legion asks you to be somebody — recruit a Londoner, wear their face, carry their story into the world. Spiderbot Arena asks you to be a thing: an eight-legged combat drone with no backstory and no idle animation to hide behind. That shift, from character to machine, is what shaped almost every screen in this case study.

About the mode
  • A fast-paced, skill-based free-for-all deathmatch
  • Players pilot a modified, weaponized version of Legion's signature spiderbot — normally a stealth/hacking tool, here turned into the whole game
  • 4 to 8 players per match, with weapons and power-ups that respawn around the arena
  • Set across three custom-built arenas carved out of familiar London locations
What I owned
  • Mapping how players discover and enter the mode from the open world
  • Squad lobby wireframes, scaling from a 4-player minimum up to a full 8
  • The spiderbot loadout / skin customization screen
  • The in-match HUD — timer, position, weapon module, scoreboard, post-match flow
  • The toast/notification system tying the mode back into Legion's hacking identity
  • Reward and retention screens for daily bonuses and live events
PROCESS — DISCOVERY

Finding the Door
Into the Arena

Before players can fight, they have to find the fight. I mapped three ways to surface Spiderbot Arena from inside the open world — each with a different relationship to Legion's fiction.

OPTION 01

Menu entry

A new row in the Online hub, next to London (free roam) and the new co-op raid. Fastest to reach — but reads like a menu, not a place.

OPTION 02

Map icon

Surface the arena as a pin on the world map. More spatial than a menu row, but still one layer removed from the streets themselves.

OPTION 03

Graffiti in the world

A spider mural players physically find and interact with on a wall — the mode discovered as a place, not selected as an option.

Entry point option 1 — a straight-forward row in the ONLINE hub, annotated over a real in-engine capture

Ten murals, hidden in plain sight

Graffiti won because it gave the mode a reason to exist inside the fiction, not just inside a menu. Ten hand-placed posters across London, visible only in online play, each one reading as DedSec street art before it reads as UI.

Discreet alleyways & impoverished areas Disabled during missions/raids Not in interiors Flat surfaces only 10 total, map-wide

Shipped in-world — a player finding the arena's spider mural mid-session

PROCESS — LOBBY & LOADOUT

Getting a Squad
Spider-Ready

The lobby

Rather than invent a new pattern, I built the lobby on top of Legion's existing squad-mission framework — the same character line-up and menu shape players already knew, with a Wardrobe entry swapped in for spiderbot loadout. Leader and non-leader states differ, and the ready-check scales cleanly from a 4-player minimum up to the full 8 — I wireframed both ends of that range to make sure nothing broke at capacity.

Prototype lobby, annotated over Legion's existing squad framework

Loadout: customize spiderbot

The skin screen needed to answer four questions at a glance: what's equipped, what's owned but unworn, what's still locked, and what's new. A white border marks the active skin, a green dot flags an owned-but-unequipped one, and empty slots stay visibly locked rather than hidden — future content should look like a promise, not a surprise.

Skin customization — locked, owned, and equipped states annotated

PROCESS — ONBOARDING

Thirty Seconds
to Learn a Spider

There's no time for a tutorial level here — players land in a lobby, then a match. The brief was one screen: forced the first time, dismissed the instant the match starts, and only three things to teach — the goal, the power-up loop, and whatever controls are unique to piloting a spiderbot.

Weapons
  • Shotgun — default weapon, powerful at close range
  • Mini Gun — high fire rate, low damage
  • Rail Gun — high-damage sniper, low fire rate
  • Rocket Launcher — fast, radial explosive projectile
Pickups
  • Overcharge — temporary speed and fire-rate boost
  • Reveal — shows nearby pickup locations
  • Health — restores health
Three arenas

Small, custom-built maps with a deliberate mix of distance and verticality, so close-range weapons and long sightlines both have somewhere to work.

Factory

Museum — "verticality at its best"

Pub — "pints and frags"

PROCESS — THE HUD

A HUD Built
to Be Glanced At

Eight players, one small readout. Every element in the arena HUD had to answer "what's happening to me, right now" without asking for a second look.

Timer / weapon module
  • Position shown as 1st–4th (later, up to 8th), not a raw number
  • Timer pulses and scales up in the final 15 seconds — a wordless urgency cue
  • Ammo shown as a count beside an infinity symbol for the base weapon
Post-match flow
  • "YOU PLACED 1st" banner holds for 5 seconds before the scoreboard takes over
  • Camera locks to a static angle for 15 seconds — no fighting for control while reading your result
Scoreboard
  • Four columns, always in order: position, name, kills, progress
  • The current player's row is always highlighted, wherever it lands
  • No empty slots — a party member leaving removes their row instead of leaving it blank
PROCESS — NOTIFICATIONS · SIGNATURE MOMENT

Every Notification
Hacks Itself Into View

Kills, pickups, taking 1st place, killstreaks — instead of a generic pop-up, every one of these routes through Legion's own scrambling-text hacking effect. It's a small thing, but it's a constant reminder that you're jacked into a drone, not just reading a HUD.

PROCESS — REWARDS & RETENTION

A Reason to Log
Back In Tomorrow

Reward module

Every match closes with a simple accounting: currency earned, and — when it happens — a named item or a new skin unlock, so a good match has something to show for itself beyond the scoreboard.

The retention loop

A short loop, deliberately: play, get rewarded, get a reason to play again tomorrow.

Play
→
Rewards
→
First match · modifiers · friend bonus
  • First daily completion — casual players get a bonus for their first game of the day; hardcore players get it for their first win
  • Gameplay modifiers — community managers can run limited-time twists (rockets-only, one-shot low-HP) at boosted rewards
  • Friend bonus — stacks 10/20/30/40% per friend in your party

How it surfaces on the mode-select tile: a gold border around the active event, "EVENT" appended to the mode's name, and bonus XP called out above the tile — so the incentive is visible before a player even opens the mode.

OUTCOME

From Wireframe to
Live Mode Select

Spiderbot Arena shipped as part of Watch Dogs: Legion's free Online update on March 9, 2021 — a 4-to-8-player free-for-all deathmatch sitting alongside the game's co-op Tactical Ops, available to every owner of the game on PS4, PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S, PC and Stadia.

The shipped mode-select screen — Spiderbot Arena front and centre

The wireframes in this case study run from the earliest "where does this even live" sketches to the shipping HUD spec. The pattern that stuck with me: almost none of the interesting UX work on an arena mode is the fighting itself — it's everything wrapped around it. How you find the fight. How you gear up for it. And how clearly the game can tell you, in half a second, what just happened to you.
